library(nlmixr2lib)

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse"))$reference`
* Description (main, zero-order gastric emptying, Model 1): `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse"))$description`
* Description (supplementary, first-order gastric emptying, Model 2): `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse_firstorder"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-10293-7> (open access; the
  Supplementary Information holds Model 2 and Tables S1-S2)

Maskawa et al. sampled feces from mice every 4 hours after a single oral dose
of vancomycin, which is essentially not absorbed from the gut, and described
the fecal concentration-time course with a minimal gastrointestinal transit
model. The stomach is a retention compartment and the cecum a mixing
compartment. In the main model (Model 1) the stomach empties into the cecum
at a constant rate `q / t_in` for a duration `t_in`. The cecum empties into
the feces by first-order transit at rate constant `k_e`. The fecal
concentration is the cecal amount divided by the mass of cecal contents `A`.
Two transit delays, stomach to cecum (`dt_SC`) and cecum to feces (`dt_CF`),
are identifiable only as their sum `t_tot`. Methods Eq. 7 gives the
closed-form fecal concentration:

    C(t) = 0                                                     for t - t_tot <= 0
    C(t) = q / (t_in A k_e) (1 - exp(-k_e (t - t_tot)))          for 0 < t - t_tot <= t_in
    C(t) = q / (t_in A k_e) (exp(-k_e (t - t_tot - t_in))
                             - exp(-k_e (t - t_tot)))            for t - t_tot > t_in

The supplementary Model 2 replaces the zero-order emptying with first-order
emptying at rate constant `k_a`. The authors found the two models comparably
good, with Model 1 slightly better by RMSE (Table S2). Both are packaged:

| Model file | Gastric emptying | Source |
|------------|------------------|--------|
| `Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse` | zero-order over `t_in` | Main text, Table 2 |
| `Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse_firstorder` | first-order at `k_a` | Supplementary Information section 2, Table S1 |

## Encoding in rxode2

The model has no plasma compartment. Its observation `Ccecum` is the fecal
concentration (mg vancomycin per g wet feces).

* **Model 1.** The gastric emptying flux `q / t_in` is a zero-order infusion
  into `cecum`, so doses go into `cecum` with `rate = -2` and
  `dur(cecum) <- d1` supplies `t_in`. `alag(cecum) <- tlag` supplies `t_tot`.
  The lag shifts the whole cecal mass curve forward by `t_tot`, not just by
  the stomach-to-cecum delay. The `cecum` state is therefore the cecal amount
  at the moment it is expelled, and `cecum / v_cecum` is exactly the
  paper's `C(t) = M_b(t - dt_CF) / A`.
* **Model 2.** Doses go into `stomach` as a bolus with `alag(stomach) <- tlag`.
  The stomach empties first-order into `cecum`.

# Population

Six male, 8-week-old conventional C57BL/6N mice were each given 0.5 mL of
vancomycin hydrochloride solution by mouth at 12:00 on day 0. Three mice
(L1-L3) received 1 mg/mL (`q = 0.5 mg`) and three (H1-H3) received 20 mg/mL
(`q = 10 mg`). Three water-only control mice were not part of the model fit.
Food and water were available ad libitum. Feces were collected every 4 h from
day -3 to day 3, then less often until day 36. Vancomycin was quantified by
solid-phase extraction and LC-MS/MS and divided by the fecal wet weight
(Methods, "Mice and fecal sample collection" and "Quantification of
antibiotics"; Fig. 1). Body weight was not reported.

The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse")()$population`.

# Source trace

Each mouse was fitted on its own (basinhopping minimisation of a squared-error
loss with a derivative penalty, `lambda = 0.9`, Methods Eq. 8). The packaged
typical values are the paper's `Mean (CV%)` row over the six mice. The
between-mouse variances are `omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2)` from the same row.

| Parameter (model) | Value | Source location |
|-------------------|-------|-----------------|
| Model 1 `ltlag` (`t_tot`) | log(5.4 h) | Table 2, Mean row |
| Model 1 `ld1` (`t_in`) | log(12 h) | Table 2, Mean row |
| Model 1 `lkfec` (`k_e`) | log(0.41 1/h) | Table 2, Mean row |
| Model 1 `lv_cecum` (`A`) | log(0.31 g) | Table 2, Mean row |
| Model 1 `etaltlag`, `etald1`, `etalkfec`, `etalv_cecum` | 0.2559, 0.3708, 0.2073, 0.3524 | Table 2, CV 54 / 67 / 48 / 65 % |
| Model 1 `addSd_Ccecum` | 0.21 mg/g | Table S2, Model1 RMSE, column 'All' |
| Model 2 `ltlag` (`t_tot`) | log(6.7 h) | Table S1, Mean row |
| Model 2 `lkst` (`k_a`) | log(0.32 1/h) | Table S1, Mean row |
| Model 2 `lkfec` (`k_e`) | log(0.36 1/h) | Table S1, Mean row |
| Model 2 `lv_cecum` (`A`) | log(0.40 g) | Table S1, Mean row |
| Model 2 `etaltlag`, `etalkst`, `etalkfec`, `etalv_cecum` | 0.1919, 0.2476, 0.2813, 0.6033 | Table S1, CV 46 / 53 / 57 / 91 % |
| Model 2 `addSd_Ccecum` | 0.60 mg/g | Table S2, Model2 RMSE, column 'All' |
| Model 1 `d/dt(cecum)`, `dur(cecum)` | n/a | Methods Eq. 2-3 |
| Model 2 `d/dt(stomach)`, `d/dt(cecum)` | n/a | Supplementary Information section 2 |
| `alag()` = `t_tot = dt_SC + dt_CF` | n/a | Methods Eq. 6-7; Supplement section 2 |
| `Ccecum <- cecum / v_cecum` | n/a | Methods Eq. 5-7 |

The per-mouse estimates used below are transcribed from Table 2 (Model 1) and
Table S1 (Model 2). The observed NCA values come from Table 1.

```{r per-mouse-params}
mice <- tibble::tribble(
  ~mouse, ~dose_group,      ~q,
  "L1",   "Low (0.5 mg)",   0.5,
  "L2",   "Low (0.5 mg)",   0.5,
  "L3",   "Low (0.5 mg)",   0.5,
  "H1",   "High (10 mg)",   10,
  "H2",   "High (10 mg)",   10,
  "H3",   "High (10 mg)",   10
) |>
  mutate(id = seq_len(n()))

# Table 2: zero-order Model 1
par_m1 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~mouse, ~t_tot, ~t_in, ~k_e, ~A,
  "L1",   4.2,    4.2,   0.35, 0.24,
  "L2",   5.0,    7.0,   0.57, 0.33,
  "L3",   3.2,    7.8,   0.66, 0.17,
  "H1",   12,     23,    0.17, 0.15,
  "H2",   4.0,    25,    0.16, 0.22,
  "H3",   4.3,    7.1,   0.58, 0.74
)

# Table S1: first-order Model 2
par_m2 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~mouse, ~t_tot, ~k_a, ~k_e, ~A,
  "L1",   4.6,    0.42, 0.62, 0.12,
  "L2",   7.7,    0.60, 0.60, 0.26,
  "L3",   3.6,    0.37, 0.37, 0.29,

)

# Table 1: observed (data-derived) fecal NCA. AUC is the trapezoidal area over
# the detection window; k_e is a log-linear regression from t_max to t_elim.
obs_nca <- tibble::tribble(
  ~mouse, ~cmax, ~aucinf.obs, ~lambda.z, ~tmax,
  "L1",   1.0,   5.6,         0.35,      8,
  "L2",   0.39,  2.9,         0.68,      12,

# The per-mouse rows reproduce the printed 'Mean' rows, i.e. the packaged
# typical values, to within the two-significant-figure printing (largest
# gap: t_in, 12.35 printed as 12).
means <- c(
  m1_t_tot = mean(par_m1$t_tot) / 5.4,
  m1_t_in = mean(par_m1$t_in) / 12,
  m1_k_e = mean(par_m1$k_e) / 0.41,
  m1_A = mean(par_m1$A) / 0.31,
  m2_t_tot = mean(par_m2$t_tot) / 6.7,
  m2_k_a = mean(par_m2$k_a) / 0.32,
  m2_k_e = mean(par_m2$k_e) / 0.36,
  m2_A = mean(par_m2$A) / 0.40
)
stopifnot(all(abs(means - 1) < 0.03))
```

The Table S1 mean of `k_a` computes to 0.327 1/h, which the supplement prints
as 0.32 (truncation rather than rounding). The packaged value follows the
printed 0.32.

# Per-mouse replication (Figure 3b and Supplementary Figure S2b)

Each mouse is simulated with its own Table 2 (Model 1) or Table S1 (Model 2)
estimates. Random effects are zeroed and the structural parameters are
overridden through `params`.

```{r per-mouse-sim}
mod1 <- readModelDb("Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse")
mod2 <- readModelDb("Maskawa_2025_vancomycin_mouse_firstorder")
mod1_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod1)
mod2_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod2)

obs_times <- seq(0, 168, by = 0.25)

# Model 1 doses enter cecum as a zero-order infusion with modelled duration.
make_events <- function(mice, cmt, rate) {
  doses <- mice |>
    transmute(id, time = 0, amt = q, rate = rate, cmt = cmt, evid = 1L)
  obs <- tidyr::crossing(id = mice$id, time = obs_times) |>
    mutate(amt = 0, rate = 0, cmt = "cecum", evid = 0L)
  bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    left_join(select(mice, id, mouse, dose_group), by = "id") |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}
ev1 <- make_events(mice, cmt = "cecum", rate = -2)
ev2 <- make_events(mice, cmt = "stomach", rate = 0)

p1 <- mice |>
  left_join(par_m1, by = "mouse") |>
  transmute(
    id,
    ltlag = log(t_tot), ld1 = log(t_in),
    lkfec = log(k_e), lv_cecum = log(A)
  )
p2 <- mice |>
  left_join(par_m2, by = "mouse") |>
  transmute(
    id,
    ltlag = log(t_tot), lkst = log(k_a),
    lkfec = log(k_e), lv_cecum = log(A)
  )

sim1 <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod1_typ,
  events = ev1, params = p1, keep = c("mouse", "dose_group"),
  rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12, maxsteps = 1e6
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(model = "Model 1 (zero-order)")
sim2 <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod2_typ,
  events = ev2, params = p2, keep = c("mouse", "dose_group"),
  rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12, maxsteps = 1e6
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(model = "Model 2 (first-order)")
sim_ind <- bind_rows(sim1, sim2) |>
  mutate(mouse = factor(mouse, levels = mice$mouse))
```

```{r figure-3b, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
sim_ind |>
  filter(time <= 96) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, Ccecum, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~mouse, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time after antibiotic administration (h)",
    y = "Fecal concentration (mg/g)",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Per-mouse fecal vancomycin profiles",
    caption = paste(
      "Replicates Figure 3b (Model 1) and Supplementary Figure S2b",
      "(Model 2) of Maskawa 2025."
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The Model 1 curves reproduce the fitted red curves of Figure 3b. In Model 1
the peak always falls at the end of gastric emptying, `t = t_tot + t_in`. The
chunk below compares the simulated peaks with the peaks of the Figure 3b
fitted curves, which the maintainers read off the published figure.

```{r figure-3b-peaks}
fig3b_peak <- tibble::tribble(
  ~mouse, ~fig_peak,
  "L1",   1.05,
  "L2",   0.385,
  "L3",   0.55,
  "H1",   17.3,
  "H2",   11.2,
  "H3",   3.25
)
peak_check <- sim1 |>
  group_by(mouse) |>
  summarise(sim_peak = max(Ccecum), t_peak = time[which.max(Ccecum)], .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(fig3b_peak, by = "mouse") |>
  left_join(par_m1, by = "mouse") |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (sim_peak / fig_peak - 1))
peak_check |>
  select(mouse, fig_peak, sim_peak, pct_diff, t_peak, t_tot, t_in) |>
  rename(
    "Figure 3b peak (mg/g)" = fig_peak,
    "Simulated peak (mg/g)" = sim_peak,
    "% diff" = pct_diff,
    "Simulated t_max (h)" = t_peak,
    "t_tot (h)" = t_tot,
    "t_in (h)" = t_in
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Model 1 per-mouse peaks vs. Figure 3b.")
# Figure reading is good to a few percent; measured |% diff| <= 5%.
stopifnot(
  max(abs(peak_check$pct_diff)) < 10,
  max(abs(peak_check$t_peak - (peak_check$t_tot + peak_check$t_in))) <= 0.25
)
```

The Model 2 curves are checked the same way against the fitted curves of
Supplementary Figure S2b. In Model 2 the peak falls at
`t_tot + log(k_a / k_e) / (k_a - k_e)`, which is `t_tot + 1 / k` when the two
constants are equal.

```{r figure-s2b-peaks}
figs2b_peak <- tibble::tribble(
  ~mouse, ~fig_peak,
  "L1",   1.23,
  "L2",   0.72,
  "L3",   0.63,
  "H1",   15.2,
  "H2",   12.7,
  "H3",   3.05
)
peak_check2 <- sim2 |>
  group_by(mouse) |>
  summarise(sim_peak = max(Ccecum), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(figs2b_peak, by = "mouse") |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (sim_peak / fig_peak - 1))
peak_check2 |>
  rename(
    "Figure S2b peak (mg/g)" = fig_peak,
    "Simulated peak (mg/g)" = sim_peak,
    "% diff" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Model 2 per-mouse peaks vs. Supplementary Figure S2b.")
stopifnot(max(abs(peak_check2$pct_diff)) < 10)
```

## Check against the closed-form solutions

Methods Eq. 7 gives the Model 1 solution in closed form. The Model 2 solution
is the Bateman function shifted by `t_tot` (Supplementary Information
section 2). In five of the six Table S1 fits `k_a` equals `k_e`, which makes
the printed `k_a q / (A (k_e - k_a))` form singular. The comparison therefore
uses its limit, `q k t' exp(-k t') / A`, when the two constants are equal.

```{r closed-form}
cf_model1 <- function(t, q, t_tot, t_in, k_e, A) {
  s <- t - t_tot
  amp <- q / (t_in * A * k_e)
  ifelse(
    s <= 0, 0,
    ifelse(
      s <= t_in,
      amp * (1 - exp(-k_e * s)),
      amp * (exp(-k_e * (s - t_in)) - exp(-k_e * s))
    )
  )
}
cf_model2 <- function(t, q, t_tot, k_a, k_e, A) {
  s <- pmax(t - t_tot, 0)
  if (isTRUE(all.equal(k_a, k_e))) {
    q * k_a * s * exp(-k_a * s) / A
  } else {
    k_a * q / (A * (k_e - k_a)) * (exp(-k_a * s) - exp(-k_e * s))
  }
}

cf1 <- sim1 |>
  left_join(par_m1, by = "mouse") |>
  left_join(select(mice, mouse, q), by = "mouse") |>
  group_by(mouse) |>
  mutate(
    cf = cf_model1(time, q[1], t_tot[1], t_in[1], k_e[1], A[1]),
    err = abs(Ccecum - cf) / max(cf)
  ) |>
  summarise(max_rel_err = max(err), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(model = "Model 1")
cf2 <- sim2 |>
  left_join(par_m2, by = "mouse") |>
  left_join(select(mice, mouse, q), by = "mouse") |>
  group_by(mouse) |>
  mutate(
    cf = cf_model2(time, q[1], t_tot[1], k_a[1], k_e[1], A[1]),
    err = abs(Ccecum - cf) / max(cf)
  ) |>
  summarise(max_rel_err = max(err), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(model = "Model 2")
cf_tab <- bind_rows(cf1, cf2)
knitr::kable(
  cf_tab |> select(model, mouse, max_rel_err),
  digits = 12,
  caption = paste(
    "Largest ODE vs closed-form difference, relative to the",
    "mouse's peak concentration."
  )
)
# Same parameters on both sides, so the difference is integration error only.
stopifnot(max(cf_tab$max_rel_err) < 1e-6)
```

## Mass balance: AUC = q / (A k_e)

Vancomycin is not absorbed, so the whole dose leaves through the cecum. The
area under the fecal concentration curve is therefore `q / (A k_e)` in both
models. PKNCA on the per-mouse simulations recovers it.

```{r pknca-individual}
nca_input <- function(sim) {
  # Floor the integrator's sub-atol undershoot and drop the numerically-zero
  # tail after the peak so that lambda.z follows the true terminal slope.
  stopifnot(all(sim$Ccecum >= -1e-6 * max(sim$Ccecum, na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE))
  sim |>
    filter(!is.na(Ccecum)) |>
    mutate(Ccecum = pmax(Ccecum, 0)) |>
    group_by(mouse) |>
    filter(time <= time[which.max(Ccecum)] | Ccecum >= 1e-6 * max(Ccecum)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    select(mouse, dose_group, time, Ccecum) |>
    mutate(mouse = as.character(mouse))
}
run_nca <- function(sim, events) {
  conc <- nca_input(sim)
  dose <- events |>
    filter(evid == 1) |>
    select(mouse, dose_group, time, amt)
  dat <- PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
    PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, Ccecum ~ time | dose_group + mouse),
    PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose, amt ~ time | dose_group + mouse),
    intervals = data.frame(
      start = 0, end = Inf,
      cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, lambda.z = TRUE
    )
  )
  PKNCA::pk.nca(dat)
}
nca1 <- run_nca(sim1, ev1)
nca2 <- run_nca(sim2, ev2)

auc_check <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(nca1) |> mutate(model = "Model 1"),
  as.data.frame(nca2) |> mutate(model = "Model 2")
) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "aucinf.obs") |>
  left_join(
    bind_rows(
      par_m1 |> mutate(model = "Model 1"),
      par_m2 |> mutate(model = "Model 2")
    ),
    by = c("model", "mouse")
  ) |>
  left_join(select(mice, mouse, q), by = "mouse") |>
  mutate(
    auc_theory = q / (A * k_e),
    pct_diff = 100 * (PPORRES / auc_theory - 1)
  )
auc_check |>
  select(model, mouse, PPORRES, auc_theory, pct_diff) |>
  rename(
    "PKNCA AUCinf (mg*h/g)" = PPORRES,
    "q / (A k_e) (mg*h/g)" = auc_theory,
    "% diff" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mass-balance check of the fecal AUC.")
# Trapezoidal error on a 0.25-h grid is well under 1%.
stopifnot(max(abs(auc_check$pct_diff)) < 1)
```

## Comparison against the observed NCA (Table 1)

Table 1 holds NCA values computed by the authors from the measured fecal
data. The simulations use each mouse's fitted parameters, so the comparison
shows how closely each individual fit reproduces its own data. It is not an
independent prediction.

```{r nca-compare-m1}
nca_units <- c(
  cmax = "mg/g", tmax = "h", aucinf.obs = "mg*h/g", lambda.z = "1/h"
)
cmp1 <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca1,
  reference = obs_nca,
  by = "mouse",
  units = nca_units,
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp1,
  caption = paste(
    "Model 1 (Table 2 per-mouse fits) vs. observed Table 1 NCA.",
    "* differs from the reference by >20%."
  )
)
```

```{r nca-compare-m2}
cmp2 <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca2,
  reference = obs_nca,
  by = "mouse",
  units = nca_units,
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp2,
  caption = paste(
    "Model 2 (Table S1 per-mouse fits) vs. observed Table 1 NCA.",
    "* differs from the reference by >20%."
  )
)
```

```{r nca-gate}
auc_vs_obs <- auc_check |>
  left_join(select(obs_nca, mouse, auc_obs = aucinf.obs), by = "mouse") |>
  mutate(pct_obs = 100 * (PPORRES / auc_obs - 1))
# Deterministic per-mouse solves: measured |% diff| is at most 14% (Model 1,
# H2) and 20% (Model 2, L1). A wrong dose, A or k_e shifts AUC by far more.
stopifnot(
  max(abs(auc_vs_obs$pct_obs[auc_vs_obs$model == "Model 1"])) < 18,
  max(abs(auc_vs_obs$pct_obs[auc_vs_obs$model == "Model 2"])) < 25
)
```

Reading the starred rows:

* **AUC** agrees to within about 15% for Model 1 and 20% for Model 2. The
  largest Model 1 difference is H2 (+14%), where the fitted plateau sits
  slightly above the 20-28 h observations (Figure 3b).
* **C_max** agrees to within 20% for every mouse under Model 1. H1 is
  highest (+19%) because the long zero-order emptying (`t_in` = 23 h) builds
  a plateau above the scattered high-dose samples. H3 is low (-17%) against
  the Table 1 value of 3.9 mg/g. Figures 2 and 3b, however, show the highest
  H3 sample at about 2.9 mg/g, so Table 1 probably misprints it. Against
  2.9 the model is 11% high.
* **t_max** in Table 1 is the time of the highest observed sample, on a 4-h
  grid. The Model 1 peak is at `t_tot + t_in`, which usually falls between
  samples. For L3, H2 and H3 it falls after the sample that happened to be
  highest.
* **Model 2** reproduces AUC equally well but is a looser fit for the peak.
  It overshoots C_max for L1 and L2 and puts t_max earlier for most mice.
  This matches Table S2, where Model 2's RMSE is higher than Model 1's for
  every mouse except L1.
* **lambda.z** (the Table 1 `k_e` column) is not expected to match. The paper
  notes that its Table 1 `k_e` comes from a log-linear regression between
  `t_max` and `t_elim`. The model `k_e` comes from fitting on the original
  scale, and the two "differ from those listed in Table 1" (Results,
  "Gastrointestinal transit model"). The simulated terminal slope equals the
  model `k_e`, by construction.

# Between-mouse variability (Figures 3c and 3d)

Figures 3c and 3d show bootstrap confidence bands, built by refitting
pooled-by-dose-group data on 80% of the time points. That procedure cannot
be rerun without the data. The chunk below shows instead what the packaged
between-mouse variability implies: 200 virtual mice per dose group, with the
90% prediction interval of the individual fecal concentration. Residual error
is excluded.

```{r vpc, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
set.seed(2025)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2025)
n_per_arm <- 200
vpc_times <- seq(0, 96, by = 1)
make_vpc_events <- function(cmt, rate) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(dose_group = "Low (0.5 mg)", q = 0.5, id = seq_len(n_per_arm)),
    tibble(dose_group = "High (10 mg)", q = 10, id = n_per_arm + seq_len(n_per_arm))
  ) |>
    (\(d) {
      bind_rows(
        d |> transmute(id, dose_group, time = 0, amt = q, rate = rate, cmt = cmt, evid = 1L),
        tidyr::crossing(d |> select(id, dose_group), time = vpc_times) |>
          mutate(amt = 0, rate = 0, cmt = "cecum", evid = 0L)
      )
    })() |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}
ev_vpc1 <- make_vpc_events("cecum", -2)
ev_vpc2 <- make_vpc_events("stomach", 0)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unique(ev_vpc1[, c("id", "time", "evid")])))

vpc <- bind_rows(
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod1, events = ev_vpc1, keep = "dose_group") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(model = "Model 1 (zero-order)"),
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod2, events = ev_vpc2, keep = "dose_group") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(model = "Model 2 (first-order)")
) |>
  mutate(dose_group = factor(dose_group, levels = c("Low (0.5 mg)", "High (10 mg)")))

vpc |>
  group_by(model, dose_group, time) |>
  summarise(
    Q05 = quantile(Ccecum, 0.05),
    Q50 = quantile(Ccecum, 0.50),
    Q95 = quantile(Ccecum, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, Q50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(dose_group ~ model, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time after antibiotic administration (h)",
    y = "Fecal concentration (mg/g)",
    title = "Median and 90% prediction interval (200 mice per dose group)",
    caption = "Compare with Figures 3c and 3d of Maskawa 2025 (a different interval)."
  )
```

```{r vpc-gate}
# Dose linearity: with no dose effect in the model, the dose-normalised
# median peak is the same in both arms up to Monte-Carlo error.
peaks <- vpc |>
  filter(model == "Model 1 (zero-order)") |>
  group_by(dose_group, id) |>
  summarise(cmax = max(Ccecum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(cmax_dn = cmax / ifelse(dose_group == "High (10 mg)", 10, 0.5)) |>
  group_by(dose_group) |>
  summarise(med = median(cmax_dn), .groups = "drop")
ratio <- peaks$med[peaks$dose_group == "High (10 mg)"] /
  peaks$med[peaks$dose_group == "Low (0.5 mg)"]
# Median of 200 draws: about 6% Monte-Carlo SE per arm, so the ratio sits
# within 0.75-1.33 with wide margin; a dose mis-scaling gives 20x or 0.05x.
stopifnot(ratio > 0.75, ratio < 1.33)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Typical values are arithmetic means of individual fits.** The authors fitted
  each mouse separately and did not fit a population model. The packaged
  typical values are the paper's `Mean (CV%)` rows in Table 2 and Table S1.
  The log-normal between-mouse variances are derived from those CVs as
  `log(1 + CV^2)`. That means the typical value sits near the mean, not the
  median, of the log-normal distribution. The CVs pool both dose groups, so
  they include the longer emptying (`t_in`) and slower cecal transit
  (`k_e`) seen in two of the three high-dose mice. The paper treats this as
  a possible dose-dependent change in gastrointestinal motility that it
  could not establish with three mice per group. The model carries no dose
  effect.
* **Residual error.** The loss function is unweighted squared error plus a
  derivative penalty (Methods Eq. 8), so the residual error is additive. Its
  SD is the pooled RMSE across the six mice (Table S2, column 'All': 0.21
  mg/g for Model 1 and 0.60 mg/g for Model 2). The pooled RMSE is dominated
  by the high-dose mice. The per-mouse RMSE of the low-dose fits is about
  0.004-0.016 mg/g, so simulating low-dose observations with the pooled SD
  overstates their noise.
* **Transit delays.** Only `t_tot = dt_SC + dt_CF` is identifiable and
  reported. The model applies it as a single lag on the cecal (Model 1) or
  gastric (Model 2) input. The paper's Model 1 stomach mass
  `M_a(t) = q (1 - t / t_in)` is not carried as a state, because the
  zero-order infusion reproduces its outflow exactly. Doses into `cecum` must
  use `rate = -2` for `dur(cecum)` to take effect.
* **Minor text-table differences.** The Results text gives the low-dose
  `t_in` range as 4.1-7.8 h and the H3 cecal content mass as 0.76 g. Table 2
  lists L1 `t_in` = 4.2 h and H3 `A` = 0.74 g. The table values are used
  here. The Table 2 means are the same either way. Table 1 lists the H3
  observed C_max as 3.9 mg/g, but the highest H3 sample in Figures 2 and 3b
  is about 2.9 mg/g. The comparison table keeps the printed 3.9. The
  observed NCA values are used only for comparison, not in the model.
* **Units.** Doses are in mg (0.5 mL of 1 or 20 mg/mL), `A` is in g of
  cecal contents, and concentrations are mg per g of wet feces, as in
  Table 1 and Figure 3.
* **Figure-derived values.** The peak concentrations of the fitted curves in
  Figure 3b and Supplementary Figure S2b, used in the per-mouse peak checks,
  were read off the published figures by the maintainers, to about +/-3%. They are used only for validation; every
  model parameter comes from Table 2, Table S1 or Table S2.
* No erratum or correction notice was found for this article as of
  2026-11-05.
